name: Threnody-Dust
specific_features: Dying microbial colonies in subsurface rock fissures
Geological evidence of a once-thriving biosphere now almost gone
description: Threnody-Dust is a barren world in mourning for the biosphere it has nearly lost. Geological evidence is unambiguous: this planet once supported extensive life, its sedimentary layers rich with trace fossils and organic compounds from an epoch when oceans covered half the surface and vegetation stabilized the continents. That era ended gradually as the atmosphere thinned and water was lost to space, leaving behind a world of eroded mountain remnants and dust-filled valleys where rivers once ran.

The thin atmosphere supports a perpetual haze of fine dust that softens the landscape into impressionistic smears of brown and gray. The dried ocean basins are the planet's most melancholic feature, their floors crusted with evaporite minerals that mark the final retreat of water from the surface. The metamorphic bedrock exposed by erosion tells the story of a geologically active past that has quieted as the planet's interior cooled, leaving it without the volcanic recycling that might have sustained its atmosphere.

Microbial life persists in subsurface rock fissures where traces of moisture remain, the last descendants of what was once a complex biosphere. These endolithic organisms metabolize slowly, their populations declining as the remaining moisture evaporates decade by decade. Xenobiologists estimate they have perhaps ten thousand years before the last colonies go silent, an endpoint that will mark the complete sterilization of a world that was alive for billions of years.

Threnody-Dust draws researchers studying planetary death, the process by which a living world becomes a dead one. The fossil record provides a detailed timeline of biodiversity collapse that correlates with atmospheric and hydrological decline, a case study applicable to understanding extinction risks on other marginally habitable worlds. There is no commercial incentive to visit beyond the scientific, and the planet's slow dying receives little attention from a civilization with more urgent concerns. The microbes in their fissures continue their ancient metabolisms, unaware that they are the last verse of a very long poem.
